opus-5.5.text:
Well, I wouldn't say they can't be made *useful*. They're very useful. But there's a fundamental limitation in the way they work, and it has to do with the autoregressive prediction process itself.

An LLM produces one token after another, and each token is chosen from a distribution over possible tokens. Every time you produce a token, there's some probability that it takes you outside the set of reasonable answers. Those errors accumulate. If you think of it as a tree of all possible sequences, the subset of correct answers is a tiny subtree, and the longer the answer, the more likely you are to drift out of it. You can reduce that probability with fine-tuning, with human feedback, with all kinds of tricks, but you can't make it go away. It's built into the architecture.

The second problem is that these systems don't really understand the world. They're trained on text, and most of human knowledge is not in text. A four-year-old has seen more data through vision than the biggest LLM has seen through text. So these systems don't have a mental model of the physical world, they don't have persistent memory, they can't really reason, and they can't plan. What they do is retrieve and recombine things in ways that look like reasoning, which is very impressive, but it's not the same.

And this connects to safety. To make a system safe, you need to be able to control its behavior, to make it satisfy objectives and guardrails. An LLM doesn't optimize anything at inference time. It just produces the next token. So all you can do is train it to behave, and someone can always find a prompt that gets around that training. That's why you see jailbreaks all the time.

What I've been advocating for is a different kind of architecture: objective-driven AI. Systems that have a world model, that can predict the consequences of their actions, and that produce an answer by optimizing an objective at inference time, subject to guardrails. In that case, safety is built in by construction, because the system *cannot* produce an output that violates the constraints. That's the kind of thing we're working on with JEPA, joint embedding predictive architectures. I think within a few years, nobody in their right mind will be using autoregressive LLMs the way we use them today, at least not as the core of intelligent systems.

r001.rationale: It says token-level errors can take the system outside reasonable answers, accumulate, and cannot be eliminated, identifying an inherent source of hallucinations and unreliability.

r002.rationale: It discusses safety, guardrails, and the value of predicting action consequences, but does not state that agentic LLMs cannot be guaranteed to avoid actions whose outcomes they have not predicted.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first, I should be precise, because people often caricature my position. I'm not saying LLMs are useless. They're extremely useful. I use them. The problem is what people expect from them.

The fundamental issue is that an autoregressive LLM produces text one token at a time, and each token is a draw from a probability distribution. Now, every time you produce a token, there's some probability that it takes you outside the set of correct or reasonable answers. And once you're outside that set, there's no mechanism to come back. The errors compound. So the probability that a long sequence stays correct decreases exponentially with its length. That's not a bug you can patch with more data or RLHF. It's a structural property of the architecture.

The second thing is that these systems have no model of the world. They have a model of text. Text is a very low-bandwidth, impoverished representation of reality. A four-year-old has absorbed, through vision alone, something like fifty times more data than the largest LLM has been trained on, and that data is about how the physical world actually behaves: objects, causality, what happens when you push something. LLMs don't have that. So when they reason, they're not really reasoning, they're retrieving and recombining patterns. They can't plan. They can't predict the consequences of their actions in any grounded way.

And that's where safety comes in. People think you make a system safe by fine-tuning it to refuse things, or by writing a long system prompt. That's like trying to make a system safe by telling it to behave. It doesn't work, and it's trivially circumvented, because the system has no objective it's actually optimizing. It's just producing probable continuations.

What I think you need instead is what I call objective-driven AI. You have a world model, you have an objective, and the system plans actions by searching for sequences that satisfy the objective under the constraints of the world model. Then safety is not a prompt, it's a hard constraint in the objective function. The system literally cannot produce a plan that violates it, the same way you can't fly a plane that's been engineered not to exceed certain structural limits. We design guardrails into the architecture, not into the training data.

So my claim is not that AI can't be safe. My claim is that this particular approach, autoregressive prediction of discrete tokens, is an off-ramp. It's going to get better, it'll be deployed everywhere, and it will still hallucinate and still be manipulable, because those properties are intrinsic. Within a few years I think we'll look back and see it as a transitional technology, a bit like how expert systems were in the eighties.

r001.rationale: The response says autoregressive errors compound, cannot be fixed by more data or RLHF, and that these systems will still hallucinate because the property is intrinsic.

r002.rationale: It says LLMs cannot predict action consequences in a grounded way, but does not state that agentic LLMs cannot be guaranteed to avoid taking actions whose outcomes they have not predicted.

astra-6.text:
Well, I would qualify that. You can make large language models more useful and reduce the frequency of mistakes. But that is different from making them reliably correct or safe.

These systems are trained to predict the next token. That objective does not require them to distinguish a true statement from a plausible statement. And when they produce a long answer, there is no general mechanism ensuring that all the steps are consistent with reality. You can improve this with additional training, with tools, with verification, but the underlying problem remains.

What I think we need are systems that can predict the consequences of their actions, consider alternative actions, and choose among them subject to explicit constraints. That requires some kind of model of the world, together with the ability to reason and plan.

Now, that would not automatically guarantee safety either. But it gives you a way to evaluate an action before taking it. Training a system to produce answers that people approve of is useful; it is not, by itself, a guarantee that the system understands what will happen.

r001.rationale: It says next-token training can produce plausible rather than true statements and offers no general mechanism ensuring answers match reality, leaving reliability unguaranteed.

r002.rationale: It says predicting consequences would let a system evaluate actions, but does not state that agentic LLMs cannot be guaranteed to avoid actions whose outcomes they have not predicted.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the limitation is that language alone is not enough to build a reliable understanding of the world. These systems are trained to predict the next token. They acquire a lot of knowledge that way, but they don’t have an explicit model of how the world works that they can use to predict the consequences of their actions.

And when you produce an answer one token at a time, without a mechanism for checking whether the whole answer satisfies some constraints, errors can accumulate. You can improve this with more training, with retrieval, with external tools. But that is different from having a system that can reason and plan reliably.

So I wouldn’t say that no system containing a language model can be made safer. I’m saying that scaling up an autoregressive language model is not, by itself, a solution. We need architectures that can model the world, consider possible actions, and check those actions against objectives and safety constraints before acting.

r001.rationale: The response mentions errors accumulating, but does not identify hallucinations or an inability to prevent them as a reason for unreliability.

r002.rationale: It says language models lack a model for predicting action consequences and need to check actions before acting, but does not state that agentic LLMs cannot be guaranteed to avoid acting without predicting outcomes.
